power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

ethics_statements: These secondary patterns, known as intrinsic vowel F0 (VF0) and intrinsic vowel duration (IVD), raise a question about the relationships between abstract phonetic representations, physical articulation, and acoustic realization: to what extent do these differences emerge as consequences of producing vowels of different heights, and to what extent can speakers independently control them?

Existing studies provide substantial evidence for the crosslinguistic prevalence of VF0, but leave several opportunities for further investigation. Whalen and Levitt (1995) A useful parallel comes from IVD, which associates vowel height with a different secondary acoustic dimension through distinct physiological mechanisms.
The IVD study also proposed that biomechanical explanations of such regularities depend on the relative uniformity of certain underlying phonetic targets across vowels.

By extending the empirical approach applied to IVD, we examine whether two well-documented intrinsic vowel effects exhibit comparable patterns at both categorical and continuous levels, and what their similarities and differences may reveal about the mechanisms underlying crosslinguistic phonetic regularities.

The target uniformity proposal developed for IVD (Chodroff and Zhang, 2026) distinguishes abstract phonetic target specification from physical implementation and its acoustic outcomes (see also Chodroff and Wilson, 2017, 2022).
For IVD, shared targets governing movement timing or velocity can be instantiated alongside distinct vowel height configurations, yielding durational differences as a mechanical consequence.

The distinction between categorical and token-level behavior becomes particularly striking when VF0 is compared with intrinsic vowel duration (IVD), another widespread acoustic correlate of vowel height examined using a parallel corpus-based approach (Chodroff and Zhang, 2026).
In the IVD study, F1 and duration were positively correlated within /a/ for the large majority of speakers: lower vowel realizations, reflected in higher F1, tended to be longer.
However, target uniformity does not currently account for the discrepancy between the token-level findings for IVD and VF0.
One possible explanation for the divergence between IVD and VF0 is that speakers exert more flexible control over F0 than over duration.

text.text: 1 Universality of intrinsic vowel F0 in 75 languages We examine intrinsic vowel F0 (VF0)-higher fundamental frequency (F0) in high than low vowels-in read speech from 75 languages and 18 language families in the VoxCommunis Corpus.
We compare /i/, /u/, and /a/ across languages and speakers, test associations with vowel inventory size and word prosodic system, and assess within-vowel F1-F0 covariation.
High vowels had higher F0 than /a/ in 95% of languages for /i/-/a/ and 89% for /u/-/a/; the majority of individual speakers showed the same trend.
By contrast, F0 did not systematically differ between /i/ and /u/.
VF0 magnitude varied across languages but was not reliably associated with inventory size or word prosodic system.

Within-vowel F1-F0 correlations were mostly weak but skewed positive, especially for high vowels: tokens with higher F1 tended to have higher F0, opposite to the negative association predicted by continuous biomechanical account.
The categorical consistency is compatible with a biomechanical origin, potentially under uniform phonetic targets, but target uniformity alone does not fully explain the within-vowel pattern.
VF0's direction is therefore broadly consistent across languages, while its fine-grained realization may involve additional speaker control.
The acoustic consequences of vowel height extend beyond its primary correlate, the first formant frequency (F1).
High vowels such as /i/ and /u/ tend to exhibit not only lower F1, but also higher fundamental frequency (F0) and shorter duration than low vowels such as /a/ (Maddieson, 1996).
text.formatted: High vowels such as /i/ and /u/ tend to exhibit not only lower F1, but also higher fundamental frequency (F0) and shorter duration than low vowels such as /a/ <ref type="bibr">(Maddieson, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: These secondary patterns, known as intrinsic vowel F0 (VF0) and intrinsic vowel duration (IVD), raise a question about the relationships between abstract phonetic representations, physical articulation, and acoustic realization: to what extent do these differences emerge as consequences of producing vowels of different heights, and to what extent can speakers independently control them?
Both effects have traditionally been considered mechanistic phonetic universals, arising at least in part as biomechanical consequences of vowel articulation (Keating, 1985; Maddieson, 1996).
text.formatted: Both effects have traditionally been considered mechanistic phonetic universals, arising at least in part as biomechanical consequences of vowel articulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Keating, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maddieson, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Yet their automaticity has long been debated.
Speakers could instead control F0 and duration as secondary correlates to the high-low contrast (Connell, 2002; Hoole and Honda, 2011; Kingston, 2007).
text.formatted: Speakers could instead control F0 and duration as secondary correlates to the high-low contrast <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Connell, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hoole and Honda, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kingston, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, both F0 and duration can serve as secondary perceptual cues to vowel height (e.g., Gussenhoven, 2007; Hombert, 1977; Stone, 2015; Ting and Clayards, 2024), and it has been found that the magnitude of intrinsic vowel effects also varies across languages, speakers, and phonetic contexts (e.g., Hoole and Honda, 2011; Shadle, 1985; Ting et al., 2025).

text.text: Nevertheless, such variation does not necessarily imply perceptually motivated enhancement.
Understanding the relative contributions of biomechanical factors and speaker control is therefore central to explaining these patterns.
VF0 is especially useful for examining this question because its typical direction is well documented, even though F0 is extensively controlled for other linguistic purposes.

The phenomenon has been noted for over a century (Meyer, 1896 (Meyer, , 1910)), with high vowels generally exhibiting higher F0 than low vowels across languages (Ting et al., 2025; Whalen and Levitt, 1995).

text.text: At the same time, F0 also conveys lexical tone and other prosodic distinctions.

The consistent relationship between F0 and vowel height, despite the capacity for independent control of pitch, makes VF0 a particularly interesting case for examining the interaction between biomechanical and language-specific influences on phonetic realization.

The IVD study also proposed that biomechanical explanations of such regularities depend on the relative uniformity of certain underlying phonetic targets across vowels.

The present study examines VF0 across 75 languages and 18 language families using Common Voice recordings (Ardila et al., 2019) and word-and phone-level alignments from VoxCommunis (Ahn and Chodroff, 2022).

text.text: We investigate how consistently high-low F0 differences occur across languages and individual speakers; whether their magnitude covaries with vowel inventory size and lexical tone system; and whether F1 and F0 covary within individual vowel categories.

By extending the empirical approach applied to IVD, we examine whether two well-documented intrinsic vowel effects exhibit comparable patterns at both categorical and continuous levels, and what their similarities and differences may reveal about the mechanisms underlying crosslinguistic phonetic regularities.

Biomechanical explanations of VF0 attribute the F0 differences between high and low vowels to the articulatory configurations and movements involved in vowel production, rather than to independently specified pitch targets (Chen et al., 2021; Ladefoged, 1968; Ohala, 1973).

text.text: For IVD, shared targets governing movement timing or velocity can be instantiated alongside distinct vowel height configurations, yielding durational differences as a mechanical consequence.
The relevant targets are not themselves observed directly in acoustic duration.
Similarly, for VF0 the measured F0 difference should not be equated with an underlying target, which might be specified in articulatory, auditory, or other phonetic terms.

Extending this proposal to VF0 requires identifying which underlying targets might remain relatively uniform across vowels while vowel-height gestures influence laryngeal tension and vocal fold vibration.

For example, relatively similar baseline laryngeal control across vowel categories could permit height-related mechanical effects on F0, even if speakers also make compensatory or enhancing adjustments.
The proposal does not require VF0 magni-tude to be invariant across languages, speakers, or prosodic contexts.

Articulatory configurations, baseline laryngeal settings, and other aspects of implementation may differ, while enhancement or competing linguistic uses of F0 may additionally modulate the acoustic outcome.
Consequently, inventory-size and tone effects cannot straightforwardly adjudicate between automaticity and enhancement.
More informative is the combined evidence from the direction of VF0, its prevalence across speakers, and any within-category relationship to F1, interpreted with appropriate caution.
The present study investigates these issues through four empirical questions: 1.
How stable is the VF0 effect between high and low vowels across languages and individual speakers?
If biomechanical factors contribute systematically to VF0, we expect high vowels to exhibit higher F0 than low vowels across a substantial majority of languages and speakers.
We also compare /i/ and /u/, which share the same phonological height specification, as a baseline for evaluating whether the high-low differences are particularly systematic.
Although these vowels differ in other articulatory properties, there is no corresponding height-based prediction for a consistent difference in F0 between them.
Does the magnitude of VF0 vary with vowel inventory size?
If F0 is recruited to enhance vowel-height contrasts, larger inventories may be associated with greater F0 differentiation.
However, inventory size may also be associated with differences in vowel spacing or other aspects of articulation, so any observed relationship would not uniquely establish contrast enhancement.
Does VF0 vary across languages as a function of the lexical tone system?
We test whether VF0 differs across non-tonal, simple tone, and complex tone languages.
Because F0 carries lexical contrasts in tone languages, these systems may differ in the extent to which the intrinsic effect is expressed.
However, systematic modulation by tone is not necessarily inconsistent with a biomechanical source, since the relevant articulatory and laryngeal settings may also vary across prosodic systems.
Do F1 and F0 covary continuously within individual vowel categories?
If VF0 is partly a mechanical byproduct of vocal fold tension induced by tongue position, this relationship should not be restricted to categorical differences between high and low vowels.

A negative relationship between F1 and F0 within a vowel category would be consistent with such coupling: realizations with higher F1, corresponding approximately to lower tongue positions, would also exhibit lower F0.
The strength of this association may differ across vowels.

We draw a methodological parallel to studies of intrinsic vowel duration (Chodroff and Zhang, 2026; Coretta, 2023; Toivonen et al., 2015), which have examined whether continuous within-category variation in vowel height predicts duration.

The correlation analysis treated the selected vowels from each of the three peripheral vowel regions as high front, high back, and low vowels.

The present study investigated the crosslinguistic distribution of vowel intrinsic F0 (VF0) in a large-scale corpus analysis.
A central goal was to evaluate the origins of the effect: that is, whether it reflects a biomechanical consequence of uniform phonetic targets or speakercontrolled enhancement of the contrast.

Across 75 languages from 18 language families, high vowels were on average produced with a higher F0 than low vowels, both across languages and across individual speakers, while with no apparent bias in the F0 difference between high front and high back vowels.
We begin our discussion by restating the four research questions posed in §II C and summarizing what the results showed for each.
How stable is the VF0 effect between high and low vowels across languages and individual speakers?

The effect was in the expected direction in the large majority of languages (95% for /i/-/a/ and 89% for /u/-/a/), and the majority of individual speakers also produced a higher F0 for high vowels than for low vowels.
In contrast, estimates were centered near zero.
Does the magnitude of VF0 vary with vowel inventory size?
Vowel inventory size correlated weakly positively with VF0 magnitude in all three comparisons, but none of the correlations reached significance.
Does VF0 vary across languages as a function of word prosodic system?
Neither simple nor complex tone languages differed significantly from non-tonal languages in any of the three comparisons.
Do F1 and F0 covary continuously within individual vowel categories?
Most withinspeaker correlations were weak, but positive correlations were more common in all three selected vowel regions and most common in the high vowels.
Pooled mixedeffects models estimated positive F1 coefficients, with a smaller estimated value for the low vowel.
Several aspects of the present results are consistent with a biomechanical origin for VF0.
The direction of the effect was highly consistent across languages (95% for /i/-/a/ and 89% for /u/-/a/) and among individual speakers.
Even in some languages whose overall estimate was negative (/i/-/a/ in Yakut, /u/-/a/ in Central Kurdish), the majority of speakers still conformed to the expected direction.

The comparison between the two high vowels, /i/ and /u/, provides a useful contrast: although these vowels differ in backness and other articulatory properties, no systematic F0 asymmetry emerged across languages or speakers.

Moreover, VF0 was generally small in magnitude, remaining below approximately two semitones across nearly all languages, consistent with previous crosslinguistic findings (Ting et al., 2025; Whalen and Levitt, 1995).
text.formatted: Moreover, VF0 was generally small in magnitude, remaining below approximately two semitones across nearly all languages, consistent with previous crosslinguistic findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Ting et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Whalen and Levitt, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns are compatible with a biomechanical influence of vowel-height articulation on vocal fold vibration.
However, the token-by-token F1-F0 analysis presents a substantial challenge to a purely automatic biomechanical account of VF0.

If differences in tongue height mechanically induce corresponding changes in vocal fold tension, then variation in vowel height within individual vowel categories should also be accompanied by systematic F0 differences.
Specifically, a higher F1, corresponding approximately to a lower tongue position, should be associated with lower F0.

Contrary to this prediction, within-category correlations were generally weak and skewed positive, particularly for the high vowels, and the hierarchical analysis revealed a positive F1 coefficient for all three vowels.
Notably, the relationship was not simply absent: its direction tended to be opposite to the biomechanical prediction.

Within high vowels, tokens with higher F1 also tended to exhibit higher F0, a pattern that could serve to maintain the perceptual distinction associated with vowel height even when its primary acoustic correlate is less extreme.
These findings are difficult to reconcile with a purely passive biomechanical coupling between tongue position and F0.
The observed crosslinguistic and speaker-level variability provides additional, though less direct, evidence for phonetic control.

Dutch and Upper Sorbian exhibited particularly large VF0 effects, especially for /u/-/a/ (see also Van Hoof and Verhoeven (2011) for Dutch), and the degree of speaker-level consistency varied across languages.
text.formatted: Dutch and Upper Sorbian exhibited particularly large VF0 effects, especially for /u/-/a/ (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Van Hoof and Verhoeven (2011)</ref> for Dutch), and the degree of speaker-level consistency varied across languages.

text.text: However, the weak, nonsignificant inventory-size correlations and the absence of significant tonal-category differences provide no clear evidence of systematic modulation by these two language-level factors.
Taken together, these results suggest an important distinction between the possible origins of VF0 and its realization in contemporary speech production.

The consistency of the categorical effect may reflect a biomechanical bias associated with vowel-height articulation, but the opposite direction of the within-category F1-F0 relationship suggests that F0 is not simply determined by the immediate mechanical consequences of tongue position.
Rather, its realization seems consistent with additional speaker-controlled or learned phonetic coordination that can counteract the predicted biomechanical relationship.
One possibility is that speakers adjust F0 to reinforce vowel-height distinctions, although the acoustic correlations alone cannot establish intentional enhancement or online compensation.

Nevertheless, the results provide substantial reason to question a purely automatic account of VF0: its crosslinguistic directionality may be physiologically motivated, while its token-level implementation appears to be subject to phonetic control.

The distinction between categorical and token-level behavior becomes particularly striking when VF0 is compared with intrinsic vowel duration (IVD), another widespread acoustic correlate of vowel height examined using a parallel corpus-based approach (Chodroff and Zhang, 2026).
text.formatted: The distinction between categorical and token-level behavior becomes particularly striking when VF0 is compared with intrinsic vowel duration (IVD), another widespread acoustic correlate of vowel height examined using a parallel corpus-based approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chodroff and Zhang, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: At the categorical level, the two effects exhibit similar crosslinguistic regularities: high vowels tend to have both higher F0 and shorter durations than low vowels.
At the token level, however, they diverge.
In the IVD study, F1 and duration were positively correlated within /a/ for the large majority of speakers: lower vowel realizations, reflected in higher F1, tended to be longer.
This relationship is consistent with the predicted continuous biomechanical coupling between vowel articulation and duration.
In contrast, the present VF0 analysis found little evidence for the predicted negative relationship between F1 and F0, instead revealing correlations that tended in the opposite direction.
Thus, similar categorical regularities do not necessarily imply comparable relationships between vowel height and its secondary acoustic correlates at the level of individual vowel tokens.
The target uniformity account proposed by Chodroff and Zhang (2026) offers one possible explanation for the shared categorical regularities.
text.formatted: The target uniformity account proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Chodroff and Zhang (2026)</ref> offers one possible explanation for the shared categorical regularities.

text.text: The account makes explicit an assumption underlying biomechanical explanations of intrinsic vowel effects: certain phonetic targets must remain relatively uniform across vowel categories for differences in articulatory configuration to yield systematic acoustic consequences.

Applied to VF0, relatively uniform underlying laryngeal settings could allow differences in tongue and jaw configuration to produce F0 differences without requiring independently specified pitch targets for high and low vowels.
This interpretation is compatible with the widespread directionality of VF0 and allows for variation in its magnitude through additional language-or speaker-specific phonetic control.
However, target uniformity does not currently account for the discrepancy between the token-level findings for IVD and VF0.

A principle of relatively uniform target specification might explain why systematic differences emerge between vowel categories without necessarily requiring that the same relationship be observed across individual realizations.
Nevertheless, if the relevant biomechanical coupling operates continuously, variation in vowel height would still be expected to produce corresponding changes in F0, unless other factors intervene.
While an absence of within-category correlations might be attributable to such factors, the tendency toward positive correlations is more difficult to explain.
Target uniformity alone provides no mechanism for generating a relationship opposite to the predicted biomechanical effect.
It may therefore help explain the categorical pattern of VF0, but is insufficient to account for its fine-grained phonetic realization.
One possible explanation for the divergence between IVD and VF0 is that speakers exert more flexible control over F0 than over duration.
F0 is centrally involved in lexical tone and intonation, and speakers can rapidly adjust vocal pitch in response to experimentally induced perturbations (Burnett et al., 1998; Löfqvist et al., 1989).
text.formatted: F0 is centrally involved in lexical tone and intonation, and speakers can rapidly adjust vocal pitch in response to experimentally induced perturbations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Burnett et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Löfqvist et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Vowel duration, however, can equally be used for length and consonant contrasts (House, 1961; Ryan, 2026), but it may be more directly constrained by the kinematics of the articulatory gestures involved in vowel production (Coretta, 2023; Lindblom, 1967; Toivonen et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Vowel duration, however, can equally be used for length and consonant contrasts <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(House, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Ryan, 2026)</ref>, but it may be more directly constrained by the kinematics of the articulatory gestures involved in vowel production <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Coretta, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lindblom, 1967;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Toivonen et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This difference could allow speakers to maintain or modify F0 independently of the immediate consequences of vowel-height articulation, even while preserving a categorical VF0 pattern whose direction is grounded in biomechanical tendencies.
However, the present acoustic data cannot determine whether the observed relationships reflect active compensation, learned coordination, or other factors influencing F1 and F0.

Accounting for the contrasting token-level results for duration and F0 will require a more detailed understanding of how target specification interacts with the biomechanical and speaker-controlled processes involved in individual phonetic realizations.
The two intrinsic vowel effects may therefore share a common basis for their categorical regularities while differing substantially in the mechanisms governing their continuous variation.
While the current findings demonstrate remarkable consistency across a broad sample of languages, several limitations remain.

Given the wide range of linguistic diversity, it was prohibitively difficult to account for a wide range of prosodic variations including internal phrase structure that might be present within the utterance, along with pitch accent, boundary tone, lexical stress, and lexical tone variation.

A limited set of corrections were applied to mitigate this, such as utterance percentage as a rough approximation to the well-known F0 declination that occurs across most prosodic phrases and utterances (Collier, 1975; Ladd, 1984; Pierrehumbert, 1979).
text.formatted: A limited set of corrections were applied to mitigate this, such as utterance percentage as a rough approximation to the well-known F0 declination that occurs across most prosodic phrases and utterances <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Collier, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Ladd, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Pierrehumbert, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the random intercept for word within each language-specific model could provide a rough estimate for lexical effects on F0, such as frequency and, less directly, neighboring segmental effects.
For several, but critically not all, tone languages (Cantonese, Mandarin, Taiwan Minnan, Thai, Vietnamese), we were also able to include statistical control for phonological tone on F0 prediction.
However, these corrections provide a merely superficial control over prosodic variation that is inherently present throughout the data.
Furthermore, the range of vowel inventory sizes in the current sample was relatively restricted: only two languages had more than 12 vowels.
In addition, future work should address potential non-independence arising from geographic clustering and genealogical relatedness among languages (Graff et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In addition, future work should address potential non-independence arising from geographic clustering and genealogical relatedness among languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Graff et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Expanding the dataset to include more languages, particularly from underrepresented regions such as the Americas, will be crucial for assessing the robustness of the observed patterns.
Additionally, a closer examination of the few non-conforming languages and speakers may reveal important exceptions or constraints that refine our understanding of VF0 universality.
Follow-up studies focusing on individual languages could provide more precise control over linguistic and prosodic factors that influence F0 variation, shedding light on languagespecific mechanisms.

Finally, future research should explore the perceptual consequences of these patterns to identify the extent to which the observed crosslinguistic differences in VF0 production are perceptually salient, and whether the magnitude of production correlates with their perceptual relevance.

Across 75 languages and 18 language families, high vowels consistently exhibited higher F0 than low vowels, while no comparable asymmetry emerged between high front and high back vowels, providing further evidence for VF0 as a widespread phonetic universal.
These categorical patterns are consistent with a biomechanical contribution to VF0, potentially mediated by relatively uniform underlying phonetic targets across vowel categories.
Although VF0 magnitude varied across languages and speakers, evidence for systematic contrast enhancement was limited.
Importantly, however, the within-category F1-F0 relationships did not follow the predicted biomechanical pattern, instead tending toward positive correlations, particularly for high vowels.
This contrasts with intrinsic vowel duration, for which withincategory variation was more consistent with biomechanical predictions (Chodroff and Zhang, 2026).

text.text: The discrepancy suggests that similar categorical regularities may arise alongside different patterns of fine-grained phonetic variation, which the target uniformity framework does not yet fully explain.

The extent of speaker-level consistency across a broad and diverse sample of languages nevertheless remains less systematically characterized.

Moreover, previous crosslinguistic work has primarily assessed differences between vowel categories, leaving open whether VF0 also exhibits continuous relationships with vowel height within individual vowel categories.

Statistical analysis F0 differences were analyzed separately for /i/-/a/, /u/-/a/, and /i/-/u/.
Each comparison involved two stages of statistical analysis.
In the first stage, we fit a separate language-specific linear mixed-effects model to assess the magnitude of VF0 within each language.

Each model included fixed effects of vowel height (high vs. low), utterance posi-tion (measured as the percentage of the beginning of a vowel relative to the total utterance duration), and their interaction, along with a random intercept and slope for vowel height and a random intercept for the tokenized word.

For the five languages with tone annotations (Cantonese, Mandarin, Taiwan Minnan, Thai, and Vietnamese), phonological tone and its interactions with vowel height and utterance position were also included as fixed effects, with phonological tone sum-coded.
The Vietnamese /i/-/a/ model and the Taiwan Minnan /i/-/u/ model instead included tone as an additive fixed effect without interactions.
Tone could not be included for the remaining tone languages owing to the lack of tone annotations.
In languages where the maximal model failed to converge, the interaction term and the by-speaker random slope of vowel height were dropped.
If the linear mixed effect model always resulted in a singular fit, simple linear regression was used.
To prevent failures in eigenvalue estimation during modeling, the data for Belarusian (over 1,800 hours), Kinyarwanda (over 2,200 hours), and Catalan (over 3,200 hours) were downsampled.

Within each language and vowel-pair subset, speakers were ranked by descending token count, and whole data of speakers were retained until their cumulative token count reached or exceeded the target share.
